# Who is on the other side?

*You'll need fills and passive orders (chapter 2), the fair value and the wall mid (chapter 3), and half the spread
against the impact (chapter 4). Fill models and resting orders are named here and explained in chapter 10; the grid and
the permutation test in chapter 11.*

## The story

Everything in the template was tuned on Prosperity data. So we took it, unchanged, into ABIDES, an independent market
simulator. Its one stock is traded by 1,000 noise agents, 102 "value" agents with noisy private views of a hidden price
that slowly returns to a mean, 12 momentum agents that follow moves, and two market makers that adapt
[(`IDEAS.md`, "An independent generator: ABIDES's RMSC04")]{.src}. ABIDES prices are in cents.

The template lost. Over ten days it made −21,798 cents (about −$218) under the most optimistic fill model, −57,872
under the strict one, and −362,428 (about −$3,624) with orders that rest. A grid of 36 of its settings, four fair
values by three quoting distances by three smoothings, found one cell that made money under the strict rule, +29,196,
and none with resting orders: the best of them lost 155,901. Under the optimistic rule seven cells made money, the best
+310,847, and that cell lost about a million resting. Doing nothing beat every cell with resting orders
[(`arena.backtest` and `arena.grid` on `data/abides`, re-run; `IDEAS.md`, "An independent generator: ABIDES's
RMSC04")]{.src}.

Then the test that explains it. We made twenty copies of the same ten days with each day's ticks put in a random
order, the same books and the same trades with no sequence, and ran a small search over the bot's quoting distance on
each. On the shuffled days the best setting made **+4,540,545 cents** on average, about +$45,000 (@fig-shuffle). On
Prosperity's Kelp the same test changes almost nothing: 27,390 credits on the real days, 27,326 on the shuffled ones
[(`data/shuffle.csv`; `IDEAS.md`, "An independent generator: ABIDES's RMSC04")]{.src}.

![The grid's best PnL on the real days and on shuffled copies: ABIDES (cents, ten days) and Prosperity 3's Kelp
(credits, three days); each panel on its own scale. Data: `data/shuffle.csv`, from `arena.grid ... --permute 20`.](../figures/f07_shuffle.png){#fig-shuffle
fig-alt="Two bar charts. ABIDES: minus 21,798 cents on the real days against plus 4.54 million on the shuffled ones. Kelp: 27,390 against 27,326."}

Shuffling keeps every book and every trade and destroys the sequence: *what happens after* each fill, including moves
that keep going. On ABIDES that was where the loss lived. The order of events was the adverse selection.

## The idea

### The fills you get are the ones you didn't want

A resting quote doesn't choose who trades with it. It is filled whenever someone finds it worth taking, and the people
most eager to take it are the ones who know the price is about to move through it. A bid gets hit just before the
price falls; an ask gets lifted just before it rises. This is *adverse selection*: conditional on being filled, a
market maker's fills are worse than its quotes looked.

The measurement is the *markout*, a fill's profit some ticks later, valued at a reference price, the mid or, on a
book like Prosperity's, the wall mid:

::: {.eq speak="a fill's markout at h ticks is how far the price moved in its favour by then: the side, times the reference price h ticks later less the fill's price"}
$$\text{markout}(h) = \text{side} \times \big(\text{ref}_{t+h} - \text{fill price}\big)$$
:::

with side +1 for a buy and −1 for a sell (`python/arena/analysis.py`, `markouts`). At the moment of the fill the markout
of a passive fill is the edge it was quoted at. On an uninformed market it stays there as h grows. Under adverse
selection it falls, and if it falls below zero the market maker pays to trade.

![The template's passive fills, volume-weighted over the days, valued against the wall mid at each number of ticks
after the fill: Prosperity 3's Kelp in credits, ABIDES in cents. Data: `data/markouts.csv`, from `arena.backtest ...
--out`.](../figures/g05_markouts.png){#fig-markouts
fig-alt="Two line charts. Kelp: plus 0.69 credits a unit at the fill, 0.68 a tick later, 0.72 after 500 ticks, flat throughout. ABIDES: plus 2.35 cents at the fill, plus 0.21 one tick later, minus 0.08 after 50 ticks and minus 0.62 after 500."}

The whole difference between the two markets is in one chart (@fig-markouts). On Kelp the template's passive fills are worth 0.69
credits a unit when they happen, 0.68 a tick later and 0.72 after 500 ticks: nothing takes the edge back. On ABIDES
they are worth 2.35 cents a unit when they happen, because the template quotes about two cents from its fair there (its
default `make_edge`, 2), and 0.21 a tick later: the price has moved two cents against them in one tick. After 50 ticks
they are below zero, −0.08, and after 500, −0.62 [(`data/markouts.csv`)]{.src}. Split by what the market did just
before, ABIDES's fills against the last move lost on every day under every fill rule, and fills with it gained
[(`IDEAS.md`, "An independent generator: ABIDES's RMSC04")]{.src}.

### Reading a markout curve

The curve is cheap to make and easy to misread, so three things about it. First, its shape says more than any one
point. A curve that stays where it started is uninformed flow. One that falls and keeps falling is informed flow, and
the horizon where it crosses zero is roughly how long the informed traders' knowledge lasts. One that falls at once and
then holds is a cost paid at the moment of trading, a jump or a stale quote, rather than someone's view.

Second, the reference price matters at short horizons. Measured against Kelp's plain mid, the same fills are worth 0.44
credits a unit at the fill and 0.67 a tick later. Nothing happened to the fills in that tick: the mid's flicker,
chapter 3's noise, is in the first number and gone from the second. Against the wall mid the curve is flat from the
start [(`data/markouts.csv`)]{.src}. On ABIDES the two differ at short horizons the other way: against the mid the
fills are already −0.32 cents a unit one tick after, −0.18 at 2 ticks and +0.12 at 20, against the wall mid's +0.21,
+0.17 and +0.13; from 50 ticks on the two agree [(`data/markouts.csv`)]{.src}. So read markouts against the fair value the bot trades around, or past the horizon where the mid's noise has
gone.

Third, a backtest's markouts depend on its fill rule, because the rule decides which fills exist. The doubtful fills,
trades printed exactly at our price between other bots, are the ones a strict rule leaves out, and DeLise's argument is
that limit-order fills come with adverse price moves, so a fill rule that treats fills as random arrivals overstates
a market maker's profit; of the four rules he replays, filling always on an adverse move plus a calibrated share of
the rest comes closest to the live simulator. The analysis tool, `arena.analysis`, prints the curve for each product with takes and passive fills apart; the passive ones are the market maker's, and the ones to watch.

### Why there is a spread at all

Adverse selection isn't only a risk to a market maker; in the classic model it is the reason the spread exists.
Glosten and Milgrom imagine a market maker who faces two kinds of taker and can't tell them apart: the uninformed, who
trade for their own reasons, and the informed, who know where the price will end up. To break even it sets its ask at
what it expects the value to be *given that someone buys*, and its bid at the value given that someone sells. Each
trade is news, so the two quotes sit apart [(Bouchaud et al., ch. 16 §16.1.1, eq. 16.1, PDF p. 319)]{.src}.

In the model's orderly case, where the uninformed traders' views are spread at least as widely as the value can move
and only a small share of traders are perfectly informed, it gives the spread in one line:

::: {.eq speak="the spread is about twice the share of informed traders times how far the value can move"}
$$s \approx 2\,\phi\,\sigma$$
:::

with [$\phi$]{speak="phi"} the share of trades that are informed and [$\sigma$]{speak="sigma"} the scale of the value's
moves [(Bouchaud et al., eq. 16.6, PDF p. 321)]{.src}. The spread grows with the share of informed traders. And if the
uninformed are too few, or trade too little when the spread is wide, there is no spread at which the market maker
breaks even: it withdraws, and the market breaks down (§16.1.4, PDF pp. 322–323). The uninformed are what pays for
everything.

Read against chapter 4's measurement, Prosperity's books are what this model calls a market with φ near zero: the
spread is wide and the price doesn't follow the trades, so the market maker keeps most of it. ABIDES has informed
traders and a one-tick spread that can't widen to pay for them, and the margin is negative.

### Two kinds of market

Prosperity's products are the friendly kind. On Kelp the takers look close to random: the template's position had a
correlation of −0.10 to +0.18 with where the price went next, about nothing. Kelp's position sits long much of the day
for a different reason: only 34 to 36% of its trades at the touch are buys, so more of its takers sell, and the bot
buys what they sell [(`IDEAS.md`, "`skew` against Kelp's long position")]{.src}. That position is the flow, not a
signal; chapter 6 tests it with a mirrored day.

ABIDES is the other kind: some traders know something, their trades move the price after them (chapter 4's impact,
1.31 cents within 50 ticks), and moves continue: after the wall mid moves 5 ticks over 20, it moves on by about 3 more
over the next 50, on all ten days [(`IDEAS.md`, "An independent generator: ABIDES's RMSC04")]{.src}. The template's
whole playbook, quote close to a fair value and wait, was built for the first kind and loses on the second. A new
market may be either, or each product may be different, which is why the repo runs a test for it before anything else
is tuned: `experiments.day.premise` combines the shuffle test, the impact and a forecast into a verdict per product,
Prosperity-like, mixed or agent-like [(`IDEAS.md`, "The premise check's verdict, calibrated on Prosperity")]{.src}.

### Being picked off

The informed need not be people. A price that jumps does the same to a resting quote. On the jumpy basket legs of
Prosperity 2 and 3, plain market making with orders that live one tick earned a few thousand credits each: Roses, on
Prosperity 2's round 3, 2,685 over three days. With orders that rest, each quote stays in the book until it fills or
is cancelled, and when the next snapshot jumps straight through it, it fills at its own stale price. Roses' wall mid
moves more than half the spread on 63% of ticks; resting, the same quotes lost 1,477,350 credits, having bought and
sold 114 thousand units that way on one day [(`arena.backtest python/bots/template.py 3 --data p2 --set
"PARAMS.ROSES={'limit': 60, 'fair': 'wall_mid', 'make_edge': 1}"` and `--resting`, re-run; `IDEAS.md`, "Market making
on products that jump, with resting orders")]{.src}.

Nobody chose to trade with those quotes because they knew something. The replay simply moved the price past them, and
a resting order is an option to trade at a fixed price, given free to whoever arrives after the price has moved. The
markout of those fills is what the jump was. The diagnose tool prints the share as its `jumps` column, and from 5% its
notes say "if orders rest, take only".

### When someone is informed, follow them

Adverse selection has a mirror image. If one trader is reliably informed, their trades are a signal. On Prosperity 3
one bot, named Olivia once round 5 showed names, traded Squid Ink six times over the round's three days, 15 lots each
time (one of them printed as two trades, with two buyers). Each buy was within 1.5 credits of that day's lowest wall
mid, and each sell within 2 of its highest (@fig-olivia). A thousand ticks after each, or at the day's close if that
came first, the price had moved her way by 4.5 to 86.5 credits; the smallest is a buy 424 ticks before the day's last
tick, and a sell 719 ticks before it is cut short the same way [(`data/olivia_trades.csv`)]{.src}. Across Kelp, Squid
Ink and Croissants none of her trades in round 5 was followed by a move against her at 100, 1,000 or 5,000 ticks; one
Kelp buy late in a day was back to no move by the close [(`IDEAS.md`, "Following informed counterparties";
`experiments.day.counterparties`)]{.src}.

![Squid Ink's wall mid over Prosperity 3's round 5, the three days end to end, with Olivia's buys and sells at their
trade prices. The line is drawn every 10th tick and every tick within 50 of a trade. Data:
`data/olivia_trades.csv` and `data/olivia_prices.csv`, from the engine's loader.](../figures/g06_olivia.png){#fig-olivia
fig-alt="A price line over three days between about 1,760 and 2,050 credits. Olivia buys 15 lots near the low of each day, at 1,772, 1,762 and 1,896, and sells 15 near each day's high, at 1,926, 1,986 and 2,047."}

Frankfurt Hedgehogs had spotted the pattern before names were shown, from trades of exactly 15 lots at a running daily
low or high, and their final Squid Ink strategy did nothing but follow it
[(`references/prosperity3-frankfurt-hedgehogs/README.md:270-319`)]{.src}. Our template's `copy` mode does the same with a
name: copying Olivia on top of plain market making took our Croissants from 1.7, 1.4 and 2.1 thousand credits a day
to 13.5, 25.9 and 20.9 thousand, and Squid Ink from 7.2, 9.5 and 6.5 to 8.9, 14.7 and 8.8. On Kelp it lost: her moves
there are small next to the market making they crowd out [(`IDEAS.md`, "Following informed counterparties";
`experiments.day.counterparties`, re-run)]{.src}. Those settings were chosen with all three days in view; chosen
leaving one day out by how often a name is right, only Olivia was picked, and following her added 54.1 thousand
credits over the held-out days, a loss on Kelp included. That rule was written after a first one, choosing names by
their mean move, had lost 399.5 thousand on the same held-out days, so it is not a clean test.

The warning is chapter 11's story. Prosperity 4's round 4 named its bots only as "Mark" and a number, and several
teams each found a different "informed" Mark. Ryan Challman's team switched theirs off when they failed on a held-out
day, and in our test no Mark with more than a handful of trades a day kept the sign of its move on all three days and
beat half the spread [(`references/wiki/contradictions.md`, row 3)]{.src}. A real Olivia is right on
every trade; a lucky one is right for two days.

::: {.callout-note title="What would differ on another market"}
On Prosperity the other side is mostly noise: markouts stay flat, the shuffle test changes nothing, and the danger is
mechanical, jumps through resting quotes. On ABIDES it is partly informed: markouts fall within a tick, fills against
the last move lose every day, and a bot that does nothing is the benchmark. On days generated by `arena.sim` with a maker quoting a tick of
noise and then replayed, per-tick fills in its usual, oscillating state gained on every day, and resting fills lost in every state
[(`IDEAS.md`, "Passive fills' value by state")]{.src}. Prosperity 3's round 5 is the one market we have where a name tells you who is informed.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="If you know ML"}
Adverse selection is selection bias with an adversary: the sample of fills you observe is chosen by the people who
profit from your errors, so it is biased in the worst direction, and more so the more visible your quotes are. The
markout curve is a calibration plot over time: how much of the edge the label "filled" really carried. The shuffle
test is a permutation test: destroy the temporal order and see whether the result needed it. Where it differs from
the usual use: here the order costing you money is the finding, not a null to reject; and copying a trader is a
feature found by searching many names, so it needs the held-out days any searched feature does.
:::

  shuffle test alone, `arena.grid ... --permute 20`.
